name: Chenille-Barrow
geological_features: Fuzzy mineral growth on rock surfaces
specific_features: Mineral whisker growths giving rocks a chenille-like fuzzy texture
Geometric mound formations of unknown origin
description: Chenille-Barrow is a small, cold barren world whose most unsettling feature is the texture of its rocks. Virtually every exposed rock surface is covered in a dense growth of mineral whiskers—needle-like crystal formations less than a centimeter long that grow perpendicular to the rock surface, giving every stone, cliff face, and boulder the fuzzy, plush texture of chenille fabric. The whiskers are composed of tin oxide, grown through a poorly understood process involving sublimation and redeposition in the near-vacuum conditions. Touching the surface with a gloved hand produces the sensation of stroking a stiff-bristled brush.

The planet's terrain is dominated by mound formations ranging from a few meters to several hundred meters in height, regularly spaced and roughly uniform in shape, resembling burial barrows arranged across the landscape by a deliberate hand. Geological analysis attributes these formations to ancient permafrost dynamics—cycles of freezing and thawing that sorted surface material into regular patterns—but the regularity is extreme enough to have generated persistent speculation about artificial origin. The mineral whiskers cover the mounds as thoroughly as they cover everything else, softening their outlines into fuzzy domes.

The permafrost beneath the surface contains embedded organic compounds of surprising complexity, suggesting that Chenille-Barrow once possessed an atmosphere and possibly supported basic chemistry approaching prebiotic conditions. These organics are preserved in the frozen ground like specimens in a museum, available for study in their original context. The compounds include long-chain hydrocarbons and aromatic ring structures that would normally break down quickly in the presence of radiation, but the permafrost has shielded them for billions of years.

Chenille-Barrow's combination of preserved prebiotic chemistry and enigmatic surface geology has attracted a small but dedicated research community. A seasonal expedition operates during the brief periods when the planet's orbit brings it close enough to its star for solar-powered equipment to function. The researchers live in temporary shelters on the fuzzy mounds, studying the organic compounds in the permafrost and debating whether the mound formations are truly natural. The whisker-covered landscape creates an oddly cozy impression for such a hostile world, every surface padded and soft-looking, a barren planet that seems to be trying to make itself comfortable for visitors who will never stay.
